q: This type-level test has passed `npm run check` for weeks. Then someone loosens `select` to accept any `string`. What happens?
options: Nothing: the check still passes, because `selct` is a typo and that is an error too
The test fails at runtime when `npm test` calls `typeChecks`
tsc reports that `colour` is not a key of PlayerState
explain: `@ts-expect-error` accepts **any** error on the next line. The misspelled `selct` doesn't exist, so the line always fails to compile, whatever `select` accepts, and the test checks nothing. That's why you write the line without the directive first and read tsc's message: here it would have said `Property 'selct' does not exist… Did you mean 'select'?`, not the error you meant. It never runs at runtime: `typeChecks` is never called.

q: You're testing "a listener that unsubscribes is never called again". Which of these are good ways to check it? Select all that apply.
options: Have the listener push into an array, emit after unsubscribing, and `assert.deepEqual` the array with what it held before
Have the listener increment a counter and assert the counter didn't change after the last emit
explain: To test a callback, make it **record** its calls, then compare the record. An array or a counter both show "not called". `doesNotThrow` passes whether or not the listener ran, and `emit` returns `undefined` either way, so neither says anything about the listener.

q: Which line correctly ports the boss lab's `expect(() => player.dispatch({ type: "pause" })).toThrow("pause: Nothing is playing")`?
options: `assert.throws(() => player.dispatch({ type: "pause" }), { message: "pause: Nothing is playing" })`
explain: `assert.throws` needs a **function** it can call inside its own try/catch, and the second argument can be an error class or an object of properties the error must have. Without the `() =>`, `dispatch` runs (and throws) before `assert.throws` is even called, so the test crashes instead of passing. `equal` and `deepEqual` compare values; they don't catch anything.

q: Put the steps of adding one new test in a good order.
items: Write the test's name as a sentence about one behaviour
Arrange, act and assert in the test body
Run it and watch it fail (or break the code on purpose)
Make it pass with the smallest change
explain: The name first keeps the test to one behaviour. Seeing it fail proves it can notice a bug; a test you've only seen green might check nothing. Then the smallest change that passes, and a commit, so the next step starts from a known-good version. None of this is about speed: one small, checked step at a time is the method.
